title: Question 5
stem:
A capacitor of capacitance $470\,\mu\text{F}$ is connected to a battery of electromotive force (e.m.f.) $24\text{ V}$ in the circuit of Fig. 5.1.

{{figure:figure_5_1}}

Fig. 5.1

The two-way switch S is initially at position X.

P and Q are identical long straight wires, each with a resistance of $5.6\text{ k}\Omega$. These wires are placed near to, and parallel to, each other. Wire Q is connected to a voltmeter.

At time $t = 0$, switch S is moved to position Y so that the capacitor discharges through wire P.

parts.label: (a)(i)
parts.text: Calculate the charge $Q_0$ on the capacitor at time $t = 0$.
hints: Hint 1: Think about the state of the capacitor just before t = 0, when the switch has been at X for a long time - what p.d. must be across the capacitor plates?
Hint 2: Remember to convert the capacitance from microfarads to farads, then combine it with the charging voltage to find the stored charge.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Spot the fully charged state**
You are sitting with the switch at X. The battery is connected directly across the capacitor, so after a long time no more charge flows and the capacitor p.d. equals the battery e.m.f., $V_0 = 24 \text{ V}$. That is the voltage that defines the initial charge.

Step 2: **Apply Q = CV**
Capacitance links charge and voltage by: $$Q = CV$$ Convert: $$C = 470 \, \mu\text{F} = 470 \times 10^{-6} \text{ F}$$ Then: $$Q_0 = (470 \times 10^{-6}) \times 24$$ $$Q_0 = 1.13 \times 10^{-2} \text{ C} \approx 0.011 \text{ C}$$

parts.label: (a)(ii)
parts.text: Calculate the current $I_0$ in wire P at time $t = 0$.
hints: Hint 1: At the instant the switch moves to Y, the capacitor acts as a 24 V source connected directly across wire P of resistance 5.6 k-ohm - what law links this voltage, resistance and current?
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Current from initial voltage**
At $t = 0$ the whole capacitor voltage appears across P. Using Ohm's law for the resistor: $$I_0 = \frac{V_0}{R}$$ $$I_0 = \frac{24}{5.6 \times 10^3}$$ $$I_0 = 4.3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ A}$$ This is the maximum current, it only falls after this instant.

parts.label: (a)(iii)
parts.text: Calculate the time constant $\tau$ of the discharge circuit.
hints: Hint 1: Recall what combination of the discharge resistance and capacitance controls how fast the discharge happens - think about the characteristic time for charge to fall to 37% of its start.
Hint 2: Check both values are in SI base units, ohms and farads, before you multiply them to get the time in seconds.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Meaning of the time constant**
$\tau$ tells you the timescale of an exponential discharge. A larger $R$ limits current and a larger $C$ stores more charge, so both slow the decay.

Step 2: **Calculate RC**
For discharge: $$\tau = RC$$ $$\tau = (5.6 \times 10^3) \times (470 \times 10^{-6})$$ $$\tau = 2.63 \text{ s} \approx 2.6 \text{ s}$$ After about 2.6 s the current has fallen to $I_0/e$.

parts.label: (a)(iv)

markscheme_points.text: line with negative gradient throughout passing through (0, $I_0$)

hints: Hint 1: Think about how the rate of loss of charge changes as the capacitor voltage drops - does the current fall quickly at first and then more slowly, or at a steady rate?
Hint 2: Remember where the curve must start on the I-axis and what value it approaches but never quite reaches for very large t.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at $(0, I_0)$ with negative gradient throughout, showing exponential decay asymptotic to the t-axis.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Shape of discharge current**
Current follows: $$I = I_0 e^{-t/\tau}$$ It is largest at $t=0$ because voltage is largest. As charge leaves, voltage falls, so current falls, which in turn slows the loss. That gives a steep start that flattens out.

Step 2: **How to draw it**
Start exactly at $I_0$ on the vertical axis. Draw a smooth curve falling with a negative gradient that gets less steep with time, never becoming flat at zero but getting closer and closer to the $t$-axis. Do not draw a straight line and do not let it touch or cross the axis.

parts.label: (b)(i)
parts.text: Explain why there is an induced e.m.f. across wire Q during the discharge of the capacitor.

markscheme_points.text: current in wire P gives rise to a magnetic field
as current (in P) changes, wire Q cuts (magnetic) flux (of wire P)
cutting magnetic flux causes induced e.m.f. (across Q)

hints: Hint 1: Start by thinking about what surrounds wire P whenever a current flows in it, even though P itself is just a resistor.
Hint 2: Now consider what is happening to that current in P during the capacitor discharge - is it steady or changing, and what does that imply for the field near the second wire Q?
Hint 3: Link a changing field through a nearby circuit to the basic law that predicts an e.m.f. without any battery or physical contact.
parts.proper_answer: Current in P produces a magnetic field around P. As capacitor discharges, current in P decreases so magnetic flux linking Q changes. By Faraday's law, changing flux linkage / cutting of flux induces an e.m.f. across Q.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Field from wire P**
Any current creates a magnetic field around it. So the discharge current in P sets up magnetic field lines that extend outwards and pass through the space around the nearby parallel wire Q.

Step 2: **Changing flux during discharge**
From part (a), the current in P is not constant, it decays exponentially to zero. Therefore its magnetic field also weakens with time, so the magnetic flux linking the loop containing Q is changing with time. You can say Q cuts the changing flux from P.

Step 3: **Faraday's law gives induced e.m.f.**
Faraday's law states that a changing magnetic flux linkage induces an e.m.f. No contact is needed. That is why the voltmeter connected to the isolated wire Q shows a reading while the discharge is happening, falling to zero when the current stops changing.

parts.label: (b)(ii)

markscheme_points.text: sketch shows line with a negative gradient throughout

hints: Hint 1: Think about when the current in P is changing fastest and when it hardly changes at all, and use Faraday's idea that e.m.f. follows rate of change, not the current itself, to decide the shape of V against t.
parts.proper_answer: Curve starting at a maximum value at t = 0 and decaying with negative gradient throughout, asymptotic to t-axis, similar exponential shape to I-t curve.
walkthrough:
Step 1: **Rate of change controls V**
Induced e.m.f. $V$ is proportional to rate of change of flux, hence to $|dI/dt|$. For exponential decay the gradient is steepest at $t=0$ and tends to zero later. So $V$ is largest at $t=0$ and then falls toward zero with a continuously decreasing negative gradient, essentially another exponential decay to the $t$-axis.
